newsitem.title: FRANCE: "Five-day" army scheme a victim of French election.
newsitem.headline: "Five-day" army scheme a victim of French election.

text.p: "Citizen's Meetings", a controversial five-day period intended to register French youths for possible future army duty and lecture them on patriotism, may never see the light of day.

Defence Ministry spokesman Pierre Servent told reporters on Thursday that the system, due for launch in a few weeks, had been delayed by the outgoing centre-right government until autumn because of Sunday's National Assembly election runoff.
The Socialist Party, tipped by many as favourite to win in the second round of the two-stage election begun last Sunday, has indicated it would scrap the system altogether if it came to power.

The "Citizen's Meetings" concept was a brainchild of Defence Minister Charles Millon who said they would maintain a link between the population and the armed forces once France's armies become entirely professional by 2002.

France has had compulsory military service for men off and on for about 200 years but President Jacques Chirac decided last year to phase it out as inefficient and because it was highly unpopular among the country's young people.

Under the "Citizen's Meetings" system, young men, and later young women as well, would be called to military centres in groups of several hundred, to undergo medical checks in case national service was to be reinstituted, and to be lectured on civic values.
In private, the hierarchy of the army forces was initially outraged at the idea, branding it a useless election gimmick without any military value that would draw on defence budgets and personnel.
There has since been a change of heart and the military now sees the the meetings as venues where youths could be recruited into the professional army.
But Socialist Party defence experts have opposed the project, complaining it would disorganise the armed forces.
